claim: Synaptotagmin 7 is one of three synaptotagmin isoforms found in all metazoans.
source: Synaptotagmin (syt) 7 is one of three syt isoforms found in all metazoans
evidence: Cited in the abstract and supported by reference to Barber et al., 2009 in the introduction

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 is ubiquitously expressed.
source: it is ubiquitously expressed
evidence: Statement in abstract without specific supporting data in manuscript

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 plays a selective and critical role in the Ca2+-dependent synaptic vesicle replenishment pathway.
source: we resolved Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent synaptic vesicle (SV) replenishment pathways, and found that syt 7 plays a selective and critical role in the Ca2+-dependent pathway
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects in Ca2+ vs Ca2+-free conditions

claim: Mutations that disrupt Ca2+-binding to synaptotagmin 7 abolish its function in synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: Mutations that disrupt Ca2+-binding to syt 7 abolish this function
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments with WT vs 4D/N mutant syt 7 shown in Figure 3

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 functions as a Ca2+-sensor for synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: suggesting that syt 7 functions as a Ca2+-sensor for replenishment
evidence: Inferred from Ca2+-binding requirement and functional data

claim: Loss of synaptotagmin 7 is phenocopied by a calmodulin antagonist.
source: we found that loss of syt 7 was phenocopied by a CaM antagonist
evidence: Demonstrated by CDZ experiments in Figures 7 and 8

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 binds to calmodulin in a highly specific and Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: we discovered that syt 7 binds to CaM in a highly specific and Ca2+-dependent manner
evidence: Shown by pull-down assays in Figure 7A

claim: The interaction between synaptotagmin 7 and calmodulin requires intact Ca2+-binding sites within synaptotagmin 7.
source: this interaction requires intact Ca2+-binding sites within syt 7
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of CaM binding with 4D/N mutant in Figure 7A

claim: A complex of synaptotagmin 7 and calmodulin serves as a key regulator of synaptic vesicle replenishment in presynaptic nerve terminals.
source: these data indicate that a complex of two conserved Ca2+-binding proteins, syt 7 and CaM, serve as a key regulator of SV replenishment in presynaptic nerve terminals
evidence: Conclusion drawn from combined biochemical and functional data

claim: Spontaneous synaptic vesicle release is unaffected in synaptotagmin 7 knockout neurons.
source: We first carried out whole-cell voltage clamp recordings using primary hippocampal neurons obtained from wild-type (WT) and KO mice and found that spontaneous SV release, measured in the presence of TTX, was unaffected in the KO neurons (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by mEPSC recordings shown in Figure 1A-E

claim: mEPSC amplitude is the same between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (WT: 20.78 ± 1.26 pA; KO: 20.46 ± 2.38 pA).
source: mEPSC amplitude (C, WT: 20.78 ± 1.26 pA; KO: 20.46 ± 2.38 pA)
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1C

claim: mEPSC charge is the same between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (WT: 116 ± 12 fC; KO: 119 ± 18 fC).
source: charge (D, WT: 116 ± 12 fC; KO: 119 ± 18 fC)
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1D

claim: mEPSC frequency is the same between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (WT: 2.32 ± 0.44 Hz; KO: 2.83 ± 0.63 Hz).
source: frequency (E, WT: 2.32 ± 0.44 Hz; KO: 2.83 ± 0.63 pA) were the same between WT and KO neurons
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1E

claim: Single action potential evoked EPSC amplitudes are unchanged in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: The EPSC amplitudes (Figure 1F–I,K–L), and the charge transfer kinetics (Figure 1J), were also unchanged in the KOs
evidence: Demonstrated by paired recordings in Figure 1F-L

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 does not function as a Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release in hippocampal neurons.
source: confirming that syt 7 does not function as Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release in hippocampal neurons (Maximov et al., 2008)
evidence: Confirmed by charge transfer kinetics data and cited previous work

claim: The Ca2+-sensitivity of single AP-evoked synaptic vesicle release is the same between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: We also examined the Ca2+-sensitivity of single AP-evoked SV release, by recording at different concentrations of extracellular Ca2+, and found that it was the same between WT and KO neurons (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: Demonstrated by recordings at varying [Ca2+]o in Figure 1K-M

claim: The paired pulse ratio is the same between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: The PPR was the same between WT and KO neurons (Figure 2B)
evidence: Shown by PPR measurements in Figure 2B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons display faster synaptic depression during high frequency stimulation.
source: KO neurons displayed faster depression during HFS (Figure 3B)
evidence: Demonstrated by HFS experiments in Figure 3B

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N Ca2+-ligand mutant, rescues the synaptic depression phenotype in KO neurons.
source: expression of WT syt 7, but not the 4D/N Ca2+-ligand mutant (which was properly folded but failed to bind Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)), rescued the depression phenotype (Figure 3B)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 3B and biochemical characterization in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The 4D/N mutant of synaptotagmin 7 is properly folded.
source: the 4D/N Ca2+-ligand mutant (which was properly folded but failed to bind Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1))
evidence: Demonstrated by CD spectra in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The 4D/N mutant of synaptotagmin 7 fails to bind Ca2+.
source: the 4D/N Ca2+-ligand mutant (which was properly folded but failed to bind Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1))
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7 and the 4D/N mutant are both present in synapses but are not well colocalized with the synaptic vesicle marker synapsin.
source: We note that WT syt 7, and the 4D/N mutant, were both present in synapses but were not well colocalized with the SV marker, synapsin, as compared to syt 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The surface fractions of synaptotagmin 7 and synaptotagmin 1 are similar.
source: The surface fractions, as well as the internal fractions, were similar between syt 1 and 7 measured by using a pHluorin tag (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Demonstrated by pHluorin imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The size of the readily releasable pool is similar between WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: The size of the RRP (the y-intercept) was similar between WT and KO neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: Calculated from cumulative charge analysis in Figure 3C-D

claim: Synaptic vesicle release probability is unchanged in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: Since single AP evoked EPSCs were identical between WT and KO neurons (Figure 1F), SV release probability (calculated by dividing the EPSC charge by the RRP size) was unchanged in the KOs (0.21 ± 0.03 for KO vs 0.24 ± 0.02 for WT).
evidence: Calculated from EPSC and RRP measurements

claim: The synaptic vesicle replenishment rate for phasic release is reduced by approximately 50% in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (0.26 ± 0.03 s−1 for KO vs 0.52 ± 0.06 s−1 for WT).
source: the replenishment rate was reduced by ∼50% for phasic release in KO neurons (0.26 ± 0.03 s−1 for KO vs 0.52 ± 0.06 s−1 for WT) (Figure 3E)
evidence: Calculated from cumulative charge analysis in Figure 3C,E

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, fully rescues synaptic vesicle replenishment in KO neurons.
source: WT syt 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, fully rescued SV replenishment (Figure 3C,E)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 3C,E

claim: The synaptic vesicle replenishment rate for tonic transmission is reduced by approximately 50% in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (2.19 ± 0.22 s−1 for KO vs 3.95 ± 0.61 s−1 for WT).
source: the replenishment rate was, again, reduced by ∼50% in KO neurons (2.19 ± 0.22 s−1 for KO vs 3.95 ± 0.61 s−1 for WT)
evidence: Calculated from tonic transmission analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5C

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescues the synaptic vesicle replenishment defect during tonic transmission.
source: WT syt 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescued this defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 5C

claim: Fast recovery of phasic release is delayed by approximately 60% in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (1.32 ± 0.22 s for KO vs 0.55 ± 0.17 s for WT).
source: fast recovery (Figure 4B) was delayed by ∼60% in KO neurons (1.32 ± 0.22 s) as compared to WT neurons (0.55 ± 0.17 s)
evidence: Calculated from recovery experiments in Figure 4A-B

claim: Slow recovery of phasic release is unaffected by loss of synaptotagmin 7 (WT: 15.72 ± 2.85 s; KO: 14.13 ± 2.24 s).
source: slow recovery (Figure 4C) was unaffected by loss of syt 7 (WT: 15.72 ± 2.85 s; KO: 14.13 ± 2.24 s)
evidence: Calculated from recovery experiments in Figure 4A,C

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescues fast recovery of phasic release.
source: WT syt 7 (0.52 ± 0.12 s), but not the 4D/N mutant (1.28 ± 0.26 s), rescued fast recovery (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 4A-B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 regulates fast recovery in a Ca2+-dependent manner during phasic release.
source: indicating that syt 7 regulates this process in a Ca2+-dependent manner during phasic release
evidence: Inferred from rescue with WT but not 4D/N mutant

claim: Recovery of total tonic transmission during high frequency stimulation displays two recovery components.
source: Surprisingly, the recovery of total tonic transmission during HFS also displayed the same two recovery components (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by recovery experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescues fast recovery of tonic transmission.
source: WT syt 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescued fast recovery of tonic transmission (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: Recovery of phasic and tonic release involves the same Ca2+-dependent pathway.
source: Thus, recovery of phasic and tonic release might involve the same Ca2+-dependent pathway.
evidence: Inferred from similar rescue patterns for both types of transmission

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons display a significant reduction in synaptic vesicle release during first fusion events in the presence of bafilomycin.
source: Under these conditions, in which SV recycling cannot play a role in ongoing synaptic transmission, KO neurons still displayed a significant reduction in SV release (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by sypHy imaging in bafilomycin in Figure 5B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons exhibit reductions in synaptic vesicle release as early as 1 second of 20 Hz stimulation.
source: KO neurons exhibited reductions in SV release as early as the second imaging time point (i.e., 1 sec, 20 Hz stimulation) (Figure 5C)
evidence: Demonstrated by early time point analysis in Figure 5C

claim: Synaptic vesicle recycling does not contribute to the observed reduction in synaptic vesicle release in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons during high frequency stimulation.
source: These data indicate that SV recycling does not contribute to the observed reduction in SV release in KO neurons during HFS.
evidence: Concluded from bafilomycin experiments in Figure 5

claim: The readily releasable pool size is the same in WT and synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons in the presence of bafilomycin (WT: 35.42 ± 5.07 pC; KO: 32.07 ± 4.54 pC).
source: The size of the RRP is the same in WT and KO neurons (WT: 35.42 ± 5.07 pC; KO: 32.07 ± 4.54 pC).
evidence: Calculated from recordings in bafilomycin in Figure 5F

claim: The synaptic vesicle replenishment rate is reduced in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons in the presence of bafilomycin (WT: 0.49 ± 0.06 s−1; KO: 0.23 ± 0.03 s−1).
source: Reduction in the SV replenishment rate in KO neurons in the presence of bafilomycin (WT: 0.49 ± 0.06 s−1; KO: 0.23 ± 0.03 s−1).
evidence: Calculated from recordings in bafilomycin in Figure 5G

claim: There are Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent pathways for synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: Together, the results thus far suggest that there are Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent pathways for replenishment
evidence: Concluded from experiments comparing Ca2+ and Ca2+-free conditions in Figure 6

claim: The readily releasable pool size is the same between Ca2+-free and physiological Ca2+ conditions.
source: Moreover, the RRP size was the same between the Ca2+-free and physiological [Ca2+]o conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose experiments in Figure 6B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 does not play a role in synaptic vesicle priming.
source: the RRP size, calculated from the first response to sucrose, was the same between WT, KO, and KOs expressing WT or the syt 7 4D/N mutant, in physiological [Ca2+]o (Figure 6B), excluding a role for syt 7 in SV priming
evidence: Inferred from unchanged RRP size in Figure 6B

claim: Recovery of the readily releasable pool is slowed by approximately 60% in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons in physiological Ca2+ (18.03 ± 2.87 s for KO vs 7.29 ± 1.05 s for WT).
source: In physiological [Ca2+]o, recovery of the RRP was slowed by ∼60% in the KOs (18.03 ± 2.87 s for KO vs 7.29 ± 1.05 s for WT) (Figure 6E)
evidence: Calculated from sucrose recovery experiments in Figure 6C,E

claim: Wild-type synaptotagmin 7, but not the 4D/N mutant, rescues readily releasable pool recovery in physiological Ca2+.
source: WT syt 7 (8.30 ± 0.79 s), but not the 4D/N mutant (20.07 ± 2.63 s), rescued this phenotype (Figure 6C,E)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 6C,E

claim: In Ca2+-free conditions, recovery of the readily releasable pool in WT neurons is reduced to the same level as observed for synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons in physiological Ca2+ conditions.
source: in Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 6D), the recovery of the RRP in WT neurons was reduced to the same level as observed for KO neurons, with or without expression of the 4D/N mutant in physiological [Ca2+]o conditions (Figure 6E)
evidence: Demonstrated by Ca2+-free experiments in Figure 6D-E

claim: Hypertonic sucrose stimulates synaptic vesicle release without increasing intracellular Ca2+.
source: Hypertonic sucrose stimulates SV release without increasing [Ca2+]i (Yao et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications

claim: The Ca2+-dependent component for recovery of the readily releasable pool in hypertonic sucrose experiments is likely due to resting intracellular Ca2+.
source: Therefore, the Ca2+-dependent component for recovery of the RRP, observed in the hypertonic sucrose experiments, is likely due to the resting [Ca2+]i.
evidence: Inferred from sucrose experiments and known properties of sucrose stimulation

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 begins to drive fusion at Ca2+ concentrations greater than 100 nM with a half-maximal concentration of 300 nM.
source: In vitro reconstitution experiments revealed that syt 7 begins to drive fusion at [Ca2+] > 100 nM ([Ca2+]½ = 300 nM) (Bhalla et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from previous in vitro reconstitution study

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 can sense resting intracellular Ca2+ to regulate Ca2+-dependent synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: Hence, it is plausible that syt 7 can indeed sense resting [Ca2+]i to regulate Ca2+-dependent SV replenishment.
evidence: Inferred from Ca2+ sensitivity data and experimental results

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 binds to calmodulin in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: robust Ca2+-dependent binding to CaM was observed only for syt 7
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays in Figure 7A

claim: Synaptotagmin 1, 2, 4, 9, and 10 do not bind to calmodulin in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: robust Ca2+-dependent binding to CaM was observed only for syt 7, demonstrating the specificity of the interaction (note: low levels of binding of syt 1, or other syt isoforms, to CaM might have escaped detection)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays in Figure 7A

claim: The Ca2+-promoted interaction between synaptotagmin 7 and calmodulin is abolished by Ca2+-ligand mutations in the 4D/N mutant.
source: Moreover, the Ca2+-promoted interaction between syt 7 and CaM was abolished by the Ca2+-ligand mutations in the syt 7 4D/N mutant (Figure 7A)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays in Figure 7A

claim: The interaction between synaptotagmin 7 and calmodulin is specific for Ca2+ as Mg2+ has no effect.
source: was specific for Ca2+ as Mg2+ was without effect (Figure 7B)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays with Mg2+ in Figure 7B

claim: The Ca2+-sensor for synaptic vesicle replenishment is a complex formed between synaptotagmin 7 and calmodulin.
source: Together, these biochemical findings are consistent with a model in which the Ca2+-sensor for replenishment is actually a complex formed between these two conserved Ca2+-binding proteins, syt 7 and CaM.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical and functional data

claim: Calmidazolium treatment reduces synaptic vesicle replenishment in WT neurons to the same level as in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: WT neurons displayed faster depression (Figure 7D, upper) and reduced cumulative phasic release (Figure 7D, lower) in the presence of CDZ, consistent with previous observations based on the calyx of Held (Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Hosoi et al., 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by CDZ experiments in Figure 7D

claim: Calmidazolium has no effect on synaptic vesicle replenishment in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: cumulative phasic and tonic release in WT neurons were reduced to the same levels as in the KO neurons, which were not affected by CDZ (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated by CDZ experiments in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Calmidazolium does not change the size of the readily releasable pool.
source: CDZ does not change the size of the RRP (Figure 7E)
evidence: Demonstrated by RRP measurements in CDZ in Figure 7E

claim: Calmidazolium reduces the replenishment rate for phasic release in WT neurons to the same level as in synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: in WT neurons, the replenishment rates for phasic (Figure 7F) and tonic release (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) were both reduced to the same levels observed for the KOs, with or without CDZ
evidence: Demonstrated by CDZ experiments in Figure 7F

claim: Calmidazolium slows the time course of fast recovery of the readily releasable pool in WT neurons, phenocopying synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons.
source: The time course for fast recovery, during phasic (Figure 8B) and tonic (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) transmission in WT neurons, was impaired, phenocopying the KO neurons which, in turn, were unaffected by CDZ.
evidence: Demonstrated by recovery experiments with CDZ in Figure 8B

claim: Calmidazolium has no effect on the time course of slow recovery of the readily releasable pool.
source: The time course for slow recovery was unaffected under all conditions tested (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by recovery experiments with CDZ in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C

claim: Calmidazolium increased the time constant for recovery of the readily releasable pool in WT neurons (20.69 ± 1.43 s vs 7.29 ± 1.05 s for controls) but had no effect on synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons (20.37 ± 2.1 s vs 18.03 ± 2.87 s for controls).
source: CDZ increased the time constant for recovery of the RRP in WT neurons (20.69 ± 1.43 s vs 7.29 ± 1.05 s for controls), but had no effect on KO neurons (20.37 ± 2.1 s vs 18.03 ± 2.87 s for controls).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose recovery experiments with CDZ in Figure 8F

claim: Calmidazolium does not compete with synaptotagmin 7 for binding to calmodulin.
source: CDZ, up to 100 µM, was simultaneously incubated with the syt 7 C2AB domain and immobilized CaM. Competition was not observed (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by competition assays in Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 and calmidazolium occupy different sites on calmodulin to regulate synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: These findings indicate that syt 7 and CDZ occupy different sites on CaM to regulate SV replenishment.
evidence: Inferred from lack of competition in binding assays

claim: Calmodulin might serve as an adaptor, linking synaptotagmin 7 to another calmidazolium-sensitive effector in the Ca2+-dependent replenishment pathway.
source: Thus, CaM might serve as an adaptor, linking syt 7 to another CDZ-sensitive effector in the Ca2+-dependent replenishment pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on non-competitive binding and functional data

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 contributes to short-term synaptic plasticity by regulating synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: In the current report, we discovered that syt 7 contributes to STP by regulating SV replenishment.
evidence: Concluded from all experimental data in the study

claim: Only synaptotagmin 1, 4, and 7 appear to be expressed in all metazoans.
source: Of the 17 syt isoforms in the mammalian genome, only syt 1, 4, and 7 appear to be expressed in all metazoans (Barber et al., 2009)
evidence: Cited from Barber et al., 2009

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 serves as a Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous synaptic vesicle release.
source: Syt 1 serves as a Ca2+ sensor for fast synchronous SV release (Geppert et al., 1994; Koh and Bellen, 2003; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004; Liu et al., 2009)
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: Synaptotagmin 4 modulates transmission by regulating neurotrophin release.
source: syt 4 modulates transmission by regulating neurotrophin release (Dean et al., 2009, 2012b)
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: Synaptotagmin 4 regulates exocytosis in the posterior pituitary.
source: also regulates exocytosis in the posterior pituitary (Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: Cited from Zhang et al., 2009

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 knock-out mice had normal synaptic transmission according to one study.
source: One group reported that Syt7 knock-out (KO) mice (hereafter termed KO) had normal synaptic transmission (Maximov et al., 2008)
evidence: Cited from Maximov et al., 2008

claim: A more recent study concluded that synaptotagmin 7 functions as a Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release.
source: but in a more recent study from the same group concluded that syt 7 functions as Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release (Bacaj et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from Bacaj et al., 2013

claim: Knock-down of synaptotagmin 7 in otherwise wild-type neurons had no effect on asynchronous release.
source: However, KD of syt 7 in otherwise WT neurons had no effect (Bacaj et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from Bacaj et al., 2013

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 regulates asynchronous synaptic transmission at the Zebrafish neuromuscular junction.
source: whereas there is evidence that syt 7 regulates asynchronous synaptic transmission at the Zebrafish neuromuscular junction (Wen et al., 2010)
evidence: Cited from Wen et al., 2010

claim: The apparent discrepancy regarding the physiological function of synaptotagmin 7 between mice and Zebrafish is likely due to species differences.
source: The apparent discrepancy regarding the physiological function of syt 7 between mice and Zebrafish is likely due to species differences, analogous to the different functions of syt 4 in Drosophila vs mice (Yoshihara et al., 2005; Dean et al., 2009; Wang and Chapman, 2010).
evidence: Inferred by analogy to syt 4 species differences

claim: Ca2+ plays an important role in the synaptic vesicle replenishment step.
source: It has been reported that Ca2+ plays an important role in the replenishment step (Dittman and Regehr, 1998; Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998; Hosoi et al., 2007; Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies

claim: Calmodulin has been implicated in synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: the ubiquitous Ca2+-binding protein CaM has been implicated in this process (Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Hosoi et al., 2007)
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: Calmodulin regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment by interacting with Munc13-1.
source: the ubiquitous Ca2+-binding protein CaM has been implicated in this process (Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Hosoi et al., 2007), by interacting with Munc13-1 (Lipstein et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from Lipstein et al., 2013

claim: Impaired replenishment of large dense core vesicles was reported in synaptotagmin 7 knockout chromaffin cells.
source: Furthermore, impaired replenishment of large dense core vesicles (LDCV) was also reported in KO chromaffin cells (Schonn et al., 2008), consistent with our current study.
evidence: Cited from Schonn et al., 2008

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 might serve as a ubiquitous Ca2+ sensor for replenishment of vesicles, including large dense core vesicles and synaptic vesicles.
source: Thus, syt 7 might serve as a ubiquitous Ca2+ sensor for replenishment of vesicles, including LDCVs and SVs.
evidence: Inferred from current study and cited chromaffin cell data

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 is likely to regulate replenishment either from the plasma membrane, or from large dense core vesicles or lysosomes.
source: So, syt 7 is likely to regulate replenishment either from the plasma membrane, or from LDCVs or lysosomes.
evidence: Inferred from localization data and functional studies

claim: pHluorin-synaptotagmin 7 does not recycle with synaptic vesicle-like kinetics, even after repetitive stimulation.
source: Moreover, pHluorin-syt 7 does not recycle with SV-like kinetics, even after repetitive stimulation (Dean et al., 2012a)
evidence: Cited from Dean et al., 2012a

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 does not traffic to synaptic vesicles before, during, or after stimulation.
source: excluding the possibility that syt 7 traffics to SVs before, during, or after stimulation
evidence: Inferred from pHluorin recycling data

claim: Calmodulin regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment via interactions with both Munc13-1 and synaptotagmin 7.
source: In molecular terms, the emerging view is that CaM regulates SV replenishment via interactions with both Munc13-1 (Lipstein et al., 2013) and syt 7.
evidence: Concluded from current study and cited work

claim: Ca2+-binding to the C2A domain of synaptotagmin 7 is endothermic.
source: Ca2+-binding to C2A and C2B was endothermic and exothermic, respectively
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Ca2+-binding to the C2B domain of synaptotagmin 7 is exothermic.
source: Ca2+-binding to C2A and C2B was endothermic and exothermic, respectively
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The 2D/N mutant C2-domains of synaptotagmin 7 do not bind Ca2+ under ITC experimental conditions.
source: neither of the mutant C2-domains appeared to bind Ca2+ under these experimental conditions
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 co-localizes with synaptic vesicles (colocalization coefficient 0.48 ± 0.03).
source: Analysis of the c-myc signals relative to the synapsin signals revealed that syt 1 (0.48 ± 0.03), but not syt 7 (0.18 ± 0.02) and syt 7 4D/N (0.19 ± 0.01), co-localized with SVs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 does not co-localize well with synaptic vesicles (colocalization coefficient 0.18 ± 0.02).
source: Analysis of the c-myc signals relative to the synapsin signals revealed that syt 1 (0.48 ± 0.03), but not syt 7 (0.18 ± 0.02) and syt 7 4D/N (0.19 ± 0.01), co-localized with SVs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: The 4D/N mutant of synaptotagmin 7 does not co-localize well with synaptic vesicles (colocalization coefficient 0.19 ± 0.01).
source: Analysis of the c-myc signals relative to the synapsin signals revealed that syt 1 (0.48 ± 0.03), but not syt 7 (0.18 ± 0.02) and syt 7 4D/N (0.19 ± 0.01), co-localized with SVs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Synaptotagmin 7 KO neurons still display faster depression during high frequency stimulation in the presence of cyclothiazide and kynurenic acid.
source: KO neurons still displayed faster depression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by recordings in CTZ and KYN in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: Cyclothiazide and kynurenic acid reduce AMPA receptor desensitization and saturation, respectively.
source: CTZ and KYN reduce AMPA receptor desensitization and saturation, respectively
evidence: Cited from Neher and Sakaba, 2001
